538.d:
It’s mind-bending how just a very simple mathematical operation such as applying a binary operator to the coordinates on a bitmap can generate such a huge collection of unique and extraordinary images.

In “binary landscapes” with just a few lines of code we use three different binary operators to the coordinates (or,xor,and) for instance (x or y) and then  divide it to another number and getting the remainder. The result is used to paint a color for this exact pixel. 

The result is a huge collection of pseudo-fractal images which evoke impossible landscapes, crowded cities, glitchy psychedelic with vivid colors or just beautiful patterns. All of them are deterministic given its initial parameters.

542.d:
A "feedback crystal" is a cellular automaton (similar to Conway's Game of Life) where the rules are represented by a randomized kernel. The kernel determines the micro and macro structures that develop in the crystal. The crystals are grown from "seed" pixels (in this artwork, the white outline and white center pixel provide the seed).

Sometimes the patterns are chaotic, sometimes they are stable. If you are lucky, a pattern will be generated "on the edge of chaos" that mixes stability and chaos in an emergent complex system. These are rare. In addition, a small number of artworks will result in "dead" crystals that do not grow. These are also rare, but there is a chance that your crystal will be a mostly black square.

Each piece is composed of 3 different randomly generated kernels that sweep outwards from the center.

580.d:
NFTemon
=======

NFTemon are unique NFT monster cards, made for battle!

Each NFTemon is a certain element type:
- Fire
- Water
- Earth
- Wind

An NFTemon has "health points" (max 999), which show how much attack points it can handle before it faints. They also have one attack with "attack points" (max 200), which show how much damage you will do. Some monsters have a lot of health, some do a lot of damage.

Each NFTemon has its own weakness type. If you get attacked by an NFTemon with your weakness element, damage is done x2.

There are unique "Rainbow" rare cards (2% chance). They have no weakness for other types and their "health" and "attack" stats are multiplied by 2. This means, they can have a max health of 1998 and could do max damage of 400.

607.d:
This procedurally generated depiction of a future Mars colony is inspired by the cover of 'The Tyranny of Distance' by Geoffrey Blainey.

*

Blainey describes the first European fleet set sail for Australia in the summer of 1787:

"The course they had followed from England amounted to some 14,000 miles and had taken eight months and a week, of which actual sailing time was six months."

Jammed into cramped quarters for six months? That's right on the money for the average time it takes NASA to send a robot to Mars – about six to eight months.

*

We can't be that far off the space-faring equivalent of the Barque sailing ships that journeyed to Australia in 1787. If the British could sail an equivalent distance in the 18th century and start a new settlement, shouldn't it be possible for us to create a Martian settlement today?

624.d:
A Voronoi field is the basis, inspired by Jonathan Reynold's "voronoi noise" sketch (available here: https://openprocessing.org/sketch/1015631 ). This starting point is used to create an abstract image that keeps drawing infinitely. Per-view randomization is introduced in the speed and size of the drawing of the arcs, to create the chaos, and in the placement of the Voronoi points. This ensures each viewing is unique. Three traits describe each individual mint:

Color: There are nine different color palettes, with "Bay" being a 20% likelihood, and all the others 10% likelihood.

Arc: This is the number of elements drawn around each point. There are three possible states, with 50 being a 10% likelihood, 5000 being a 20% likelihood, and 500 being the default at 70%. 

Resolution: This is the number of points in the Voronoi field. There are four candidates, with 1 being the least likely (10%), 2 and 10 having a 20% likelihood of occurring, and 5 being the most common at 50%. 

Created in p5.js

Reminiscent of festive Christmas tree baubles while tripping on acid at the family get together, this generative and animated piece creates shapes based on the standard Penner easing equations. Usually these equations are used to add a real-world feel to objects in motion. Here are they used to create symmetrical patterns, overlayed with each other in a circular world. 

For each token,  colours, number of shapes, starting positions, rates of movement and mathematical equation are generated, resulting in unique generative patterns for each minted item. 

Will you get “Space” with “easeInOutBounce” with 1 bauble and 6 waves? Or “70s Flares”, “easeInElastic” with 8 baubles and 3 waves? Or even “Striptease Neon”, “easeOutBack” with 5 baubles and 8 waves? … Who knows? 

Created with code by AutoEclectus, November 2021.

657.d:
A further extrapolation of my operation 01 piece. Intentional errors are introduced. Per-view randomization is in the speed and size of the drawing of the arcs, and in the placement of the Voronoi points. Each viewing is unique, but each mint is also unique. 

The image draws in its entirety in about 10 seconds. After 20 seconds, it clears, randomizes the placement, and draws again. Full-screen capable.

Three traits describe each individual mint:

Color: There are nine different color palettes, with "Bubblegum" being a 20% likelihood, and all the others 10% likelihood.

Arc: This is the number of elements drawn around each point. There are three possible states, with 300 being a 10% likelihood, 3000 being a 20% likelihood, and 1500 being the default at 70%.

Resolution: This is the number of points in the Voronoi field. There are four candidates, with 2 being the least likely (10%), 3 and 4 having a 20% likelihood of occurring, and 5 being the most common at 50%.

658.d: Taking inspiration from work by Karl Gerstner, Armin Hofmann, Nick Kuder and Dmitri Cherniak, PEGS explores the limits of constrained algorithmic variation. Based on the simple, playful idea of wrapping a string across a board of pegs, it shows how endless possibilities can be achieved with just a basic set of rules and a few primary colors. When done right, generative art challenges us to answer fundamental questions around creativity, beauty, and life itself.

719.d: Moonstruck is a charming film filled with the beauty of filial piety that embodies Italian culture. It is lighthearted yet peppered with a morbid tone to keep you on your toes. Though it is clear that the symbolism of the moon is outdated and irrelevant, there are strong messages in the film. The over-the-top yet matured moments by Cher makes for a good chuckle while the green Nicholas Cage is a sight to behold. The real beauty in this film lies in the veteran actors that bring much personality and flair to their individual characters. From Rose's morning coffee to her brief encounter with a kind professor; she represents a mother with experience and maturity. Her father's inner conflict with himself is frustrating yet comical. All in all, a movie that will indeed appeal to many after a long time.
